title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Tucson, AZ: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Tucson defense, copper mining and structural steel inspectors: Part C code choice, Part B travel, eligibility.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in Tucson: Six Days for Defense Manufacturing, Copper Mining and Structural Steel Inspectors
html:
Tucson's welders work for customers who rarely appear in the same sentence. Missile production on the south side of the city, copper and molybdenum mines along the Santa Cruz valley, aircraft storage and regeneration at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, and the steel frames going up for schools, hospitals and warehouses across Pima County all depend on welds that someone has to judge against a written standard. For a growing share of that work, the person doing the judging is expected to hold the American Welding Society's Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) credential, or to be working toward it.

Atlantis NDT prepares Tucson candidates for the CWI examination with a six-day course: welders and fitters stepping into quality roles, shop inspectors at fabricators and machine builders, NDT technicians who want the welding credential beside their method certifications, and engineers who sign off fabrication. The American Welding Society writes and administers the exam and decides who becomes certified. Each candidate files an individual application with AWS and has to satisfy its experience, education and vision rules in person. The course has no AWS approval or endorsement, and nobody at Atlantis has seen a live exam question. There is no Atlantis classroom in Tucson. The six days can be taken online at your own pace with an instructor answering your questions, delivered at an employer's plant or yard for a group, or booked one-to-one, online or in person at a location agreed when you book. The national CWI course page sets out what each day covers.

Defense production, stored aircraft and a fabrication shop with eight decades behind it

Raytheon, the RTX business that builds missiles, bases its missile operation in Tucson. In February 2026 the Arizona Technology Council reported that output there would ramp up over several years under new agreements with the Department of War covering Tomahawk, AMRAAM, Standard Missile-6 and Standard Missile-3 variants, with some agreements aiming at two to four times the existing production rates and RTX planning investment in facilities and workforce to reach them. Expansions of that kind mean new and rebuilt buildings, equipment and utilities, and every structural frame, pipe rack and handling fixture that comes with them is welded work that somebody has to inspect.

Across town, the 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group occupies about 2,600 acres of Davis-Monthan Air Force Base on Tucson's southeast side. The Air Force describes it as storing roughly 3,200 aircraft and 6,100 engines, reclaiming parts for the operating fleet and returning stored aircraft to flying service. Most of that is mechanical work, but a base and storage operation of that size also has structures, ground equipment and utilities that need welding and repair.

Heavy fabrication has deep roots here as well. CAID Industries, an Arizona corporation since 1947 and part of Samuel, Son & Co. since 2018, runs more than 230,000 square feet of production and office space on a 25-acre site in Tucson and offers engineering, fabrication, machining, automation and installation. The AWS Arizona Section held its January 2026 meeting at the plant, by then trading as Samuel Advanced Fabrication, with a tour of the shop floor. Shops like that one are where a CWI checks fit-up, weld size and profile, welder qualifications and records long before anything ships.

Copper country south and southeast of the city

Drive south on Interstate 19 and the mining industry is hard to miss. Freeport-McMoRan's 2025 annual report describes its Sierrita mine, about 20 miles southwest of Tucson, as a wholly owned open-pit copper and molybdenum complex in operation since 1959. In October 2026 Hudbay Minerals and its partner Mitsubishi Corporation approved construction of the Copper World mine on the west slope of the Santa Rita Mountains, southeast of the city, with production slated for 2029 and around a thousand construction jobs expected before then.

A mine is a welding job that never really ends. New projects need concentrator buildings, conveyor galleries, crusher supports, tanks, thickeners and slurry and water pipelines. Operating mines need repair on a constant basis: worn chutes and liners, cracked equipment frames, hardfacing on buckets and truck beds, and structural members that take vibration and impact on every shift. Structural work usually follows AWS D1.1, repairs to mobile equipment often follow the manufacturer's procedure, and process piping for water, reagents and tailings is normally specified to an ASME B31 code. An inspector who knows which document governs each of those jobs, and who can find its acceptance criteria quickly, is valuable to the mine owner and to every contractor on site.

Special inspection on Tucson building projects

On commercial buildings, welding inspection connects to the building permit through special inspection. The City of Tucson's special inspection certificate cites Section 1704 of the International Building Code as the city has adopted it. The owner acknowledges on the form that special inspection will take place on its behalf, a registered architect or engineer takes responsibility for the inspections and certifies them complete before a certificate of occupancy is issued, and the building official approves the qualifications of each special inspector. Inspection reports are filed with the building official.

Because the form leaves qualification to the building official, the credential an inspector needs for structural steel welding is settled jurisdiction by jurisdiction and project by project. Ask the testing agency you work for, or hope to join, what it puts forward for welding special inspection, and if building work is your goal, plan around AWS D1.1 for Part C.

Matching the Part C code book to Southern Arizona work

Part C, Code Application, is an open-book test on a single code that you name when you apply. The editions on the AWS initial application in November 2026 included AWS D1.1:2020, API 1104 22nd edition, AWS D1.2:2014 for structural aluminum, AWS D1.5:2020 for bridges, AWS D15.1:2019 for railroad work, AWS D17.1:2024 for aerospace fusion welding, and an ASME option that combines Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3. Pick the one you will actually work from:

Your Tucson workBook that usually fitsReason
Building steel, special inspection, mine structures and conveyor galleriesAWS D1.1The structural acceptance criteria, joint details and welder qualification rules you will use every week
Defense or aerospace hardware built to a fusion welding specificationAWS D17.1Written for aerospace fusion welding; confirm first that your customer's drawings invoke it
Process, water and tailings piping at mines and plantsASME option (Section IX, B31.1, B31.3)Procedure and welder qualification plus piping examination and acceptance
Gas transmission and distribution pipelinesAPI 1104Pipeline welding procedures, welder tests and acceptance standards
Highway bridges for state or county ownersAWS D1.5Bridge fabrication and inspection requirements beyond D1.1

Whichever book you choose, buy the edition AWS lists, tab it while you study and practise finding tables against the clock; day four of the course is spent inside it. Background reading: AWS D1.1, D1.1 weld acceptance criteria, ASME Section IX and ASME B31.3.

The Arizona Section and welding programs in Tucson

Southern Arizona members belong to the AWS Arizona Section, Section 055. The section is based around Phoenix but does bring meetings south, as its January 2026 shop tour in Tucson showed, so a Tucson candidate can meet working inspectors, hear technical talks and ask about the exam without always making the drive up Interstate 10. Contact details are on the section's page at sections.aws.org.

Pima Community College runs Tucson's main credit welding program at its Downtown Campus. The college lists a one-semester Basic Welding certificate built on shielded metal arc welding, blueprint reading and field techniques, a one-year Fabrication Welding certificate covering structural, ornamental and exotic metalwork, and a two-year Associate of Applied Science in Welding whose content runs from oxy-fuel cutting to robotic welding, with metallurgy and drafting along the way. All three are taught in person. For a future CWI the choice of route matters, because AWS credits welding education against the years of experience it requires and an associate degree counts for more than trade courses. AWS decides how a particular program is classed, so keep your transcripts with your application papers.

Getting to Part B from Tucson

Part A, Fundamentals, is a 150-question computer-based test, and Part C is also computer-based; both are booked at a Prometric site once AWS accepts your application and sends the eligibility code Prometric asks for, and Prometric's locator shows the sites closest to Tucson. Part B, the Practical, is the part that means travel. AWS gives it only where it holds its educational seminars, and its list of CWI training locations in November 2026 contained no Arizona city. Los Angeles was the nearest, a long day's drive west on Interstate 10, with Denver next. AWS requires at least 72 percent on each part, so book Part B early enough that a retake would still fit your plans, and check the AWS seminar and exam schedule for dates before you fix a study timeline. Related pages: CWI exam prep in Los Angeles and CWI exam prep in Phoenix.

Preparing around shifts, summer heat and long commutes

Tucson's industrial work is spread out: a mine shift near Green Valley, a fabrication job close to the airport, a building site on the northwest side. The online format turns the six-day outline into a plan you follow at your own speed, with course notes, original practice questions and timed practice papers, and you send questions to the instructor whenever something will not come clear. A sensible split for shift workers is to keep the calculation-heavy material, such as fabrication math, heat input and welding symbols, for days off, and use shorter evenings for code-book drills and discontinuity identification.

Part B tests hands and eyes, so practise with real gauges on real welds. Fillet weld gauges, an undercut gauge, a bridge cam gauge and a pair of calipers will tell you more about your readiness than any number of photographs. The Practical NDT welding workshop lets you rehearse visual inspection steps in a browser, the free NDT practice tests cover the nondestructive testing content of Part A, and the article on CWI results by exam part shows where candidates tend to lose marks.

Six days at a Tucson plant, shop or mine maintenance yard

When a Tucson employer has several people heading for the exam, the corporate format brings the six days to its premises. A fabricator can use its own production welds and rejected parts on the practical day. A mine maintenance contractor can bring in worn and repaired components so the group can discuss discontinuities and repair quality on the steel it actually works with. An engineering or testing firm can center the code day on AWS D1.1 and the special inspection reports its people write. The employer chooses the weeks, which usually means avoiding a shutdown or a project peak.

The employer's part ends with the course. Each person in the group applies to AWS separately, passes the vision examination, documents their own experience and sits every part of the exam in their own name, even when the company pays the fees.

Building a Tucson work history that AWS will accept

AWS sets the minimum years of welding-related experience by education level. A bachelor's degree in welding engineering or welding technology calls for one year, and an associate degree or higher in welding, engineering technology, engineering or a physical science calls for two. Engineering or technical courses that apply toward a welding bachelor's call for three, completed trade or vocational courses for four, and a high school diploma or equivalent for five, rising to nine years with eighth-grade schooling and twelve with less. The experience has to be verifiable, and AWS decides what qualifies.

Southern Arizona careers often combine very different jobs, which makes good records important. A welder who worked mine maintenance, then a fabrication shop, then a season on a pipeline should list each employer with dates, the processes used, the codes or specifications the work followed and any inspection-type duties, such as checking fit-up, keeping weld maps or recording welder qualifications. Ask former supervisors early whether they will confirm the work. Defense and aerospace employees should check what they are allowed to describe and keep descriptions general where a program is restricted.

Vision is tested separately. A qualified eye-care or medical professional completes the AWS visual acuity form, which covers near vision of Jaeger J2 or equivalent at no less than 12 inches, corrected if necessary, and color perception. AWS limits how far ahead of the exam that test may be taken, so schedule it close to your exam window. The CWI requirements guide explains the rules in more depth, and the CWI exam budget calculator helps you include the Part B trip in your plans.

What a Tucson CWI can add next

A new CWI in Tucson usually starts on structural, fabrication or mine work. Inspectors who want to perform tests as well as judge welds add method certifications, which come from training and certification by their employer under its written practice. Atlantis offers training based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A for that purpose, such as VT Level 2, MT Level 2 for crack detection on welds and UT Level 2 for volumetric examination, and the employer certifies the technician afterwards. Inspectors heading toward refineries and process plants elsewhere in the Southwest may look at the API inspector programs; Atlantis offers self-paced API inspector exam preparation, and API administers those exams and issues the certificates.

The CWI runs on a nine-year cycle, with renewal applications at the third and sixth years and a choice of recertification routes at the ninth, including retaking Part B or documenting 80 professional development hours. Local pages: NDT training in Tucson, aerospace NDT training in Tucson, ultrasonic testing in Tucson, magnetic particle testing in Tucson and ultrasonic testing for mining.

What to include in a Tucson enquiry

Say whether the course is for one person or a group and which of the three formats suits you, name the code book you are leaning toward for Part C, and give a rough idea of when you want to sit the exam. For an on-site group, add the location, the number of people and any weeks to avoid. If you are unsure whether your experience qualifies, a short summary of your work history lets us point out what to check with AWS before you start. Fees are quoted on request. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is there an AWS section that meets in Tucson?
faq.a: Tucson members belong to the AWS Arizona Section, Section 055, which is based in the Phoenix area but holds some of its meetings in Tucson. Its January 2026 meeting was a shop tour at Samuel Advanced Fabrication on South Tucson Boulevard. Contact details are on the section's page at sections.aws.org.

faq.q: Where would a Tucson candidate sit Part B?
faq.a: Part B is given only where AWS runs a CWI seminar. The AWS training locations list in November 2026 had no Arizona city, and Los Angeles and Denver were the nearest. Parts A and C are taken at a Prometric site, and Prometric's locator shows the closest ones to Tucson.

faq.q: Which Part C code book suits mine work around Tucson?
faq.a: For mine structures, conveyors and plant steel, AWS D1.1. If your work is mainly process, water or tailings piping, the ASME option combining Section IX, B31.1 and B31.3 may suit you better. Repairs to mobile mining equipment often follow manufacturer procedures, which are not a Part C choice.

faq.q: Should someone working for a defense supplier choose AWS D17.1?
faq.a: Only if the customer drawings and specifications you work to invoke it. D17.1:2024 covers aerospace fusion welding and is on the AWS list, but welded fixtures, handling equipment and buildings at defense sites more often follow D1.1 or a customer specification. Check what you actually inspect before choosing.

faq.q: Does the City of Tucson require special inspectors to be CWIs?
faq.a: The city's special inspection certificate does not name a credential. Under Section 1704 of the International Building Code as Tucson has adopted it, the building official approves each special inspector's qualifications, so ask the jurisdiction and your testing agency what they accept for structural welding.

faq.q: I studied welding at Pima Community College. How much experience will AWS want from me?
faq.a: That depends on how AWS classes what you completed. An associate degree in welding brings the requirement down to two years of welding-related work, and completed trade or vocational courses bring it to four, against five with a high school diploma alone. Send your transcripts with the application so AWS can decide.

faq.q: Can a Tucson fabricator run the course for its own inspectors?
faq.a: Yes. In the corporate format the six days are delivered at the employer's site and can use its production welds, gauges and qualification records. Every participant still applies to AWS individually and sits the examination personally.

faq.q: Does completing the course make me a CWI?
faq.a: No. The course prepares you for the examination; AWS administers it and certifies candidates who meet its requirements and reach at least 72 percent on each part. Atlantis has no AWS approval or endorsement.

faq.q: What should a Tucson quote request contain?
faq.a: The number of people, the format you prefer, your likely Part C code and the period when you plan to test. Use the enquiry link on this page. Fees are quoted on request, and a reply comes within one business day.
